description: This is box elder, acer negundo, also known as the boxelder maple. Box elder has sap that can be collected and turned in to a syrup similar to maple syrup. This one is relatively young as we can see in the image how close to the ground these leaves are growing and how small they are. Speaking of the leaves, box elder leaves can help identify the species. They have a unique shape that features 3 distinct peaks with serrated edges, the middle peak always being the largest and the other 2 range in size but are usually rather small. The weather at the time of this observation was sunny and 60 degrees. The humidity was around 44% with the high being 62 degrees and the low 30. With this weather information we know that box elder can live in a range of climates as we are seeing a high and low today with a 32 degree temperature difference and we have also had various weather elements this week including snow and rain. There were many other trees in the area including but not limited to: Norway Spruce (Picea abies), Norway Maple (Acer platanoides), Pin Oak(Acer platanoides), and Tulip Tree (Liriodendron). Box elder trees produce these seed pods, unfortunately there is not one pictured, but several squirrel and bird species eat the seeds from these trees. While they do foster positive interactions such as providing food to birds and squirrels they are also the likely home to box elder bugs which tend to damage gardens, crops, and are an annoyance in general.

description:
I found this visually interesting old dried pair of samaras (winged fruits) in a mixed Maple, Oak, Beech wood in southwestern Pennsylvania, elevation around 299 meters (980 feet), near the floodplain of a medium size creek, just above a manmade lake. This was along a disused roadbed in former farmland, and near some planted pines as well (some pine needles are in the photo).

I have always associated these "whirlybird" seeds with Maples, but am not sure if one can identify these fruits as to species by their shape alone, or whether one needs to examine the flowers or leaves, etc. to tell them apart. 

I ignorantly assume that most native Maples here must be Sugar Maples, but I think there are Norway, Silver, and Red Maples in some parts of the county. It is hard for me to tell how much of these particular woods are truly native trees, or human influenced.

description:
This tree in flower before the leaves are fully out reminded me of the Sugar Maples we had near the house on the farm, but were clearly not the same species. But, perhaps related? What is related to a Maple, but not a Maple? 

A Boxelder of course. 

I knew very little about Boxelders when I started to notice them at this location. I knew that they are native to this area, and sometimes produce thickets along streams that are important cover for wildlife. 

They are, unusually for a Maple, dioecious, so individual trees are either male or female. This one, I think, has female flowers, and so will go on to produce the Maple-like paired winged seeds, "samaras," through the summer.

description:
Another small (maybe 5 meters) tree in mid-October that was very heavily laden with fruit, in this case, cascades of linked winged samaras that, when detached, spin beautifully in the air like a helicopter's motorized wing. The shear number of these wondrously shaped elegant pairs of wings make such a crop a significant percentage of the female tree's annual material production. I wonder how many there are on this one tree alone - thousands, tens of thousands? They were so thick that they seem to outnumber the number of actual leaves the tree could have produced. Mind boggling, and quite beautiful I think. I just love the shape of the wings for some reason. 

This was on a gentle open slope overlooking a re-engineered floodplain just above a dam-like flood control structure in the valley of the Enlow Fork of Wheeling Creek. This localized much altered landscape is being recolonized by some native trees and shrubs, including a large number of American Sycamores lower down. This tree is a native species, and I assume it was planted by nature rather than human engineers, but the environment around the dam is clearly far from undisturbed. Nearby, upstream, is a splendid large area of relatively undisturbed naturally evolving mixed deciduous woodland on steeper slopes. This incredible tree was growing at an elevation of around 275 meters (902 feet).

description:
https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/article/2003/4-1-2003/redstain.html

Boxelder, Acer negundo, is sometimes identified by a red stain in the wood. The presence of the stain does not seem to harm the structure of the wood. In fact, some people find the stain interesting and incorporate it into woodworking projects. The color of the stain can range from light pink to dark red. When exposed to the light, the color of the stain fades over time.

It has been reported that the stain is caused by the infection of the fungus Fusarium reticulatum. A recent study, however, gives evidence that the cause of this staining may be related to nonspecific causes, particularly wounding caused by environmental factors, insect injury, or sapsucker injury.

description: The Boxelder, scientifically known as Acer negundo, is a species of maple tree native to North America. Despite its common name, the Boxelder is distinct from other maples and is often considered a weed tree due to its rapid growth and propensity to colonize disturbed areas. This deciduous tree typically grows to a moderate size, reaching heights of up to 50 feet, with a spreading canopy of compound leaves. The leaves are composed of three to seven leaflets with serrated edges and a light green color, turning yellow in the fall before dropping from the tree. Boxelder trees are dioecious, meaning they produce separate male and female flowers on different trees. The flowers are small and inconspicuous, appearing in clusters in early spring before the leaves emerge. Female trees produce winged seeds, known as samaras, which are dispersed by the wind. Despite its status as a weed tree, the Boxelder has some value as a shade tree and is sometimes planted in urban areas for its tolerance of poor soil and urban pollution. However, it can also be invasive in some regions, competing with native vegetation for resources. As I observed the Boxelder in its natural habitat, I couldn't help but appreciate its tenacity and adaptability, even in less-than-ideal conditions.

The common name indicates the resemblance of the foliage to that of elders (Sambucus) and the whitish wood to that of Box (Buxus sempervirens L.).
